In spite of substantial progress, persistent challenges such as genotype dependency, limited transformation efficiency, low reproducibility, and regulatory constraints continue to hinder the large-scale application of transgenic soybean technologies. Henceforth, emerging strategies including gene stacking, genome editing, and advanced vector systems are discussed as promising approaches to overcome these limitations. Agrobacterium-mediated transformation is a valuable tool for functional genomics and soybean improvement. Its integration with genome-editing technologies, systems biology, and conventional breeding can accelerate the development of climate-resilient, nutritionally enhanced soybean cultivars.

title: Knowledge-based injection molding optimization framework under real manufacturing constraints
source: The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology
summary: Injection molding parameter selection requires the simultaneous balancing of product quality, cycle time, and process stability. The inconsistencies among shop-floor, polymer datasheet, plastic simulation, and Subject Matter Expert (SME) re
content: Injection molding parameter selection requires the simultaneous balancing of product quality, cycle time, and process stability. The inconsistencies among shop-floor, polymer datasheet, plastic simulation, and Subject Matter Expert (SME) recommended parameters may lead to uncertainty and impractical solutions in real manufacturing. Existing optimization and simulation-based approaches fail to account for this issue, thereby limiting industrial applicability. Consequently, this study proposes a knowledge-based integrated framework for robust and industry-applicable parameter optimization. The methodology employs Grey Wolf Optimization (GWO) as the primary optimization tool to perform global exploration and local exploitation of process parameters within defined bounds and ideal targets, as well as under constraint-driven conditions without predefined ideal values based on surface-finish requirements. Taguchi analysis and regression modeling are utilized to identify important parameters and provide statistical validation. The results demonstrate that melt temperature is the primary factor governing sink marks and cooling time, while mold temperature primarily controls volumetric shrinkage, confirming thermally driven process behavior. Although both parameter ranges, namely SME-guided theoretical ranges defined prior to production and SME-adjusted practical ranges used at the shop floor, originate from SME knowledge, they differ due to presumptions versus real process conditions. By incorporating these practical SME constraints into the GWO search, the framework achieves near-zero deviation, including 0% deviation in injection pressure, $$-3.45\%$$ in mold temperature, $$+0.18\%$$ in melt temperature, $$-8.33\%$$ in hold time, $$-11.11\%$$ in cooling time, and $$-6.94\%$$ in cycle time, from shop-floor conditions while effectively balancing quality and productivity, thereby enabling stable and industry-ready parameter selection. Further independent shop-floor validation showed close agreement with the GWO recommendations and achieved acceptable quality within three gate-seal trials.

title: Feedbacks between natural climate solutions and plant invasions
summary: Abstract Biological invasions and carbon sequestration guide many modern-day land management decisions. However, intersections between invasions and natural climate solutions (NCS) - actions to maintain or increase the land carbon sink - ha
content: Abstract Biological invasions and carbon sequestration guide many modern-day land management decisions. However, intersections between invasions and natural climate solutions (NCS) - actions to maintain or increase the land carbon sink - have not received adequate attention in either the invasion or climate mitigation literature. We therefore review how plant invasions affect NCS and vice versa, focusing on reductions in emissions and carbon removals associated with avoided habitat conversion, restoration, forest and cropland management, agroforestry, and optimal grazing. We find that plant invasions can interfere with rapid NCS implementation and reduce the durability of carbon storage in many systems, although there are cases in which invasive plants increase carbon storage, creating biodiversity-climate mitigation trade-offs. At the same time, studies find that several NCS increase community resistance/resilience to invasions, and do so in forests, in particular, which can suppress invasive species spread in these systems. These dynamics suggest a positive feedback loop between NCS and invasions, in which NCS facilitate invasion control, and successful invasion control, in turn, eases further NCS implementation. This feedback could accelerate gains in land-based carbon storage and generate co-benefits for biodiversity, provided that NCS projects receive resources for sustained invasive species management. We highlight areas in need of further research, including how financial mechanisms for climate action could be used to overcome invasion-induced implementation barriers.

title: Beyond ROI: the sustainability paradox of tourism investment in Sub-Saharan Africa—A critical systematic review of readiness, governance, and just pathways
summary: Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) holds extraordinary natural and cultural heritage yet captured less than 2% of global tourism foreign direct investment (FDI) between 2010–2024, representing US$8–12 billion in annual lost development finance. This
content: Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) holds extraordinary natural and cultural heritage yet captured less than 2% of global tourism foreign direct investment (FDI) between 2010–2024, representing US$8–12 billion in annual lost development finance. This critical systematic review asked not merely why investment remained low, but whose development was served, at what cost, and under what conditions tourism advanced sustainable outcomes. Synthesizing 124 academic studies and 53 gray literature documents published between 2000 and 2024, the review identified six binding constraints: land tenure insecurity (73% of sources), restrictive visas (67%), infrastructure deficits (61%), corruption (58%), profit repatriation (52%), and licensing burdens (44%). Empirical evidence on sustainability outcomes remained limited, only 18% of academic studies reported sustainability-related data, with literature dominated by capital flows rather than community wellbeing or ecological integrity. To address this gap, the study introduced the Sustainable Tourism Investment Readiness (STIR) framework, reframing investment readiness around three pillars: pro-poor outcomes, ecological limits, and procedural justice. Evidence from patient capital (US$1.4 billion committed in 2023, growing at 26.8% annually) and technology-enabled ventures (seed investments US$250,000–1.5 million, internal rate of returns (IRRs) 18–45%) demonstrated that alternative approaches could align financial returns with sustainability. Such alignment required governance reforms prioritizing community land tenure, equitable benefit-sharing, and institutional accountability. The investment–sustainability paradox is solvable, but not through technocratic ease-of-doing-business reforms alone. Visa liberalization, land tenure reform, and tourism zones could improve viability by 3–5 percentage points, yet without social safeguards and ecological conditionality they risk reinforcing enclave tourism, leakage, and dispossession. The review proposed a research agenda centered on sustainability-grounded metrics and offered actionable recommendations for investors, policymakers, and development finance institutions (DFIs) seeking to align capital with just and sustainable development.

title: Biodiversity safeguards ecosystem services and functions worldwide
summary: Abstract Biodiversity loss threatens ecosystem services on which humanity depends, yet the strength, form and context-dependency of biodiversity–ecosystem service and biodiversity–ecosystem function relationships remain poorly quantified. H
content: Abstract Biodiversity loss threatens ecosystem services on which humanity depends, yet the strength, form and context-dependency of biodiversity–ecosystem service and biodiversity–ecosystem function relationships remain poorly quantified. Here we synthesize 423 studies to determine how biodiversity affects ecosystem functioning and service delivery. We show that regulating services, including water quality and pollination, often exhibit linear relationships, suggesting an additive role for diversity. While biodiversity enhances most functions and services, our effect-size analysis shows that oceanic ‘blue carbon’ sequestration is exceptionally sensitive, revealing how critical marine biodiversity is for climate mitigation. Conversely, services such as hazard regulation appear relatively insensitive to biodiversity, instead depending on a few functionally unique foundational species whose persistence nonetheless is interdependent on the wider community. Our new synthesis enables the forecasting of impacts, for example, that biodiversity loss will reduce pest regulation in countries experiencing population growth and intensive development, and it also highlights how ecosystem services might be used to anticipate future problems.

title: Summer oxygen dynamics in the bottom waters of a wide, temperate shelf sea
summary: Abstract. Seasonal depletion of dissolved oxygen (DO) in stratified shelf seas has important consequences for benthic and pelagic ecosystems and biogeochemical cycling. There is a need to understand the importance of different processes con
content: Abstract. Seasonal depletion of dissolved oxygen (DO) in stratified shelf seas has important consequences for benthic and pelagic ecosystems and biogeochemical cycling. There is a need to understand the importance of different processes contributing to the bottom water oxygen budget, and how those processes might change in a warmer ocean. Using CTD observations from the UK Shelf Sea Biogeochemistry programme, we construct a summer DO budget for the bottom waters of the Celtic Sea and use the budget to assess how bottom water DO might change in a warmer climate. Across the shelf, bottom water DO concentration declined during summer stratification, with greater losses in shallow northern waters and slower depletion in deeper southern regions. At a well-sampled site in the central Celtic Sea, the bottom water shows a consistent net DO loss of –44 ± 4 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹. Respiration and remineralization dominate this decline (–54 ± 19 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹), while vertical turbulent fluxes from the subsurface chlorophyll maximum (SCM) form an important DO source (30 ± 17 mmol m-2 d-1). Episodic wind events enhance DO supply from the SCM, helping to offset some of the DO consumption in the bottom water. Benthic oxygen demand and horizontal transports make minor contributions to the DO budget. A +2 °C “business as usual” climate warming will reduce oxygen solubility and lead to a 12 mmol m-3 drop in DO concentration in the bottom water over the summer stratified period. However, we find that increased microbial metabolic rates in the warmer bottom water are more important for changes in bottom water DO concentrations, potentially driving a decrease in DO concentration of about 35 – 66 mmol m-3. Combined, these effects will lead to increased oxygen deficiency in the central and northern Celtic Sea. Our results demonstrate the importance of metabolic responses to a warmer ocean, but also the need to better understand changes in winds and wind-driven mixing across the seasonal thermocline.

title: Measuring large-scale mCDR using a novel Atmospheric CO₂ Perimeter Flux (ACPF) method
summary: Achieving net-zero CO₂ emissions globally requires an annual removal of on the order of 7–9 Gt CO₂; but current CO₂ removal (CDR) measurement methodologies are not designed to quantify marine CDR (mCDR) at the megaton-to-gigaton scales requ
content: Achieving net-zero CO₂ emissions globally requires an annual removal of on the order of 7–9 Gt CO₂; but current CO₂ removal (CDR) measurement methodologies are not designed to quantify marine CDR (mCDR) at the megaton-to-gigaton scales required for climate relevance. This perspective presents a new methodology, the Atmospheric CO₂ Perimeter Flux (ACPF) method, an atmospheric-domain framework for the monitoring, reporting, and verification (MRV) of marine carbon dioxide removal. ACPF relies on a network of autonomous surface vehicles (ASVs) that monitor CO₂ concentration and wind vector in the well-mixed marine boundary layer (MBL) above the mCDR region. The sensors integrate net CO₂ mass flux in the MBL across the perimeter in tonnes per hour. Paired upwind and downwind ASVs track the sampled air mass, suppressing synoptic-scale CO₂ variability common to both ends of the transect. The difference between upwind and downwind CO 2 values can be converted into XCO₂ difference values comparable to satellite retrievals. The framework constrains net surface exchange over the enclosed region without ocean-interior observations or a biological-pump model. Attributing that exchange to an intervention requires a baseline obtained by the same array, over the same region. The magnitude of the signal that ACPF must resolve is assessed against the surface CO₂ depletion implied by the post-Pinatubo atmospheric anomaly. The ACPF architecture applies to any bounded mCDR intervention that generates a measurable surface CO₂ depletion at the megaton-to-gigaton-per-year scale required by today’s net-zero commitments.

title: Safeguarding old-growth and primary forests: protection and forest landscape restoration to deliver Europe’s 30×30 commitments
summary: Safeguarding old-growth and primary forests is essential for biodiversity conservation, climate regulation, ecosystem resilience and cultural heritage, yet these forests remain rare, fragmented and increasingly threatened across the EU. Rec
content: Safeguarding old-growth and primary forests is essential for biodiversity conservation, climate regulation, ecosystem resilience and cultural heritage, yet these forests remain rare, fragmented and increasingly threatened across the EU. Recent assessments estimate that primary and old-growth forests represent <3% of EU forest extent, with substantial gaps in spatially explicit mapping; this rarity underscores the urgency of protection and evidence-based restoration strategies (European Commission 2021b; Sabatini et al., 2018 ). In alignment with the EU Biodiversity Strategy for 2030, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (Target 3, “30×30”) and the EU Nature Restoration Regulation, this paper argues for a dual pathway: (i) protection and improved legal enforcement for remaining intact, high-integrity old and primary forests and (ii) forest landscape restoration (FLR) to strengthen buffer zones, recover old-growth attributes and reconnect landscapes (CBD, Convention on Biological Diversity, 2022; European Union, 2024). We outline governance strategies to harmonize implementation across scales and emphasize the role of participatory management, engaging landowners and communities to strengthen social legitimacy and reduce pressures on remaining forests. Additionally, we suggest practical restoration frameworks, such as the Restoration Opportunities Assessment Methodology (ROAM), that support evidence-based interventions. We conclude with priority actions for conserving primary forests, restoring ecological connectivity, and communicating the ecological, cultural, and socio-economic values of old-growth landscapes. By coupling protection with landscape-scale restoration, supported by robust social safeguards and monitoring, Europe can accelerate progress toward 30×30 targets while enhancing climate resilience and societal benefits.

title: Geographically close nearshore sites exhibit contrasting dissolved oxygen dynamics and ecosystem metabolism in eastern Lake Taihu
summary: Diel dissolved oxygen (DO) dynamics integrate biological metabolism and physical forcing and provide a powerful tool for investigating ecosystem metabolism in shallow lakes. However, whether geographically close sites exhibit similar metabo
content: Diel dissolved oxygen (DO) dynamics integrate biological metabolism and physical forcing and provide a powerful tool for investigating ecosystem metabolism in shallow lakes. However, whether geographically close sites exhibit similar metabolic behavior and environmental controls remains poorly understood. Here, three years (2022–2024) of high-frequency DO observations from three contrasting nearshore sites in eastern Lake Taihu were used to quantify diel and seasonal variability in net ecosystem production (NEP), gross primary production (GPP), and ecosystem respiration (R). Yidixuan (YDX) is strongly influenced by surrounding anthropogenic activities, Yuyangwan (YYW) has comparatively stable environmental conditions, and Xintiandi (XTD) is subject to an intermediate level of disturbance. All three sites exhibited clear diel cycles in DO and NEP but differed markedly in oxygen level, diel amplitude, and metabolic balance. YYW maintained relatively high DO, small diel fluctuations, and predominantly positive NEP, whereas XTD and especially YDX showed lower DO, larger diel oxygen oscillations, and predominantly negative NEP. At YDX, the pronounced diel oxygen amplitude suggested intensified oxygen turnover, with respiration exceeding production overall. XGBoost-SHAP analysis revealed site-specific environmental associations with NEP. Photosynthetically active radiation was the primary predictor at YYW, pH was the leading predictor at XTD, and oxidation–reduction potential and pH were most influential at YDX. Comparison of the two respiration formulations showed that their performance depended strongly on local DO regime, with the direct nighttime formulation performing more consistently under relatively stable oxygen conditions and the alternative formulation providing more interpretable estimates where diel oxygen variability was large. These results demonstrate that substantial ecological differences can occur among nearby nearshore sites within a single shallow lake and highlight the value of diel DO dynamics for understanding metabolic variability and guiding metabolism estimation in freshwater ecosystems.

title: Old-growth beech forests - Joint Natural Heritage of Europe
summary: ncient trees are witnesses of cultural and natural history. Old-growth forests are like the “backbone” or “lungs” of the Biosphere. The beech (Fagus sylvatica) is a miracle tree, and beech forests are an outstanding example for adaptation t
content: ncient trees are witnesses of cultural and natural history. Old-growth forests are like the “backbone” or “lungs” of the Biosphere. The beech (Fagus sylvatica) is a miracle tree, and beech forests are an outstanding example for adaptation to diverse site conditions and for resilience in changing environment. The expansion of beech from their glacial refuge areas to large parts of our continent, the succession of beech forests, the change from mixed deciduous forests to beech dominated deciduous forests, and the co-evolution with the cultural history in Europe is a fascinating story. And, as a specific European phenomenon beech forests promote a common European identity. The inscription of European Beech forests in the UNESCO World Heritage List improves the public awareness for the value and importance of virgin forests and supports the movement for the protection of remaining old-growth forests in Europe.

title: ECOLOGICAL RELATIONS OF NATURAL REGENERATION OF FOREST PHYTOCOENOSES IN THE LEFT-BANK POLISSIA OF UKRAINE
summary: This study aimed to identify the factors affecting the population density, viability, and structural stability of natural regeneration in leading forest species (Pinus sylvestris, Quercus robur, Acer platanoides) in the Left-Bank Polissia o
content: This study aimed to identify the factors affecting the population density, viability, and structural stability of natural regeneration in leading forest species (Pinus sylvestris, Quercus robur, Acer platanoides) in the Left-Bank Polissia of Ukraine. The research focused on four forest formations: Pineta sylvestris, Querceta roboris, Betuleta pendulae, and Populeta tremulae. Field surveys used stratified random sampling and elemental accounting of self-seeding cohorts. Key environmental factors influencing cohort conditions included soil water regime, nitrogen content, carbonates, habitat illumination, and thermal regime. The study revealed how cohort traits respond to gradients of these factors, showing both diversity and individuality, which are crucial for enhancing adaptive potential and environmental sustainability. The response of these young cohorts to ecological factors reflects species-specific regeneration requirements and their ability to adapt. In Pineta sylvestris hylocomiosa forests, conditions for successful natural regeneration were found to be favorable. However, anthropogenic pressure led to a 35-55% reduction in regeneration density, decreased vitality, and cohort imbalance. The study also found that natural regeneration is more cost-effective than plantation forestry, reducing costs by 2.3-3.5 times per hectare. These findings can inform sustainable forest management and predict forest ecosystem adaptability to climate change. Keywords: biodiversity; ecosystems; natural regeneration; integrated population analysis; population structure; mathematical modelling.

title: Psychotropic drugs in drinking water? A scoping review of evidence on diazepam and fluoxetine
summary: The global prevalence of mental disorders has increased considerably in recent decades. This evidence, associated with population growth and the expansion of access to medications, favors the growing global consumption of psychotropic drugs
content: The global prevalence of mental disorders has increased considerably in recent decades. This evidence, associated with population growth and the expansion of access to medications, favors the growing global consumption of psychotropic drugs. Consequently, an increasing load of these substances is introduced into the environment, especially into water bodies, characterizing them as emerging contaminants. This scoping review study aimed to integrate data and provide a global overview of the occurrence of widely used psychotropic drugs (diazepam, fluoxetine, and haloperidol) in drinking water. The search for studies was conducted across 7 databases, with no language or publication year restrictions. We included only original studies in this review and synthesized data from the included studies for water sampled, sampling location, year of sampling, analytical method used, psychotropic drug found, and concentration found. Our review identified 13 studies published between 2000 and 2024 on the occurrence of diazepam and fluoxetine in tap water, drinking water, bottled water, and drinking well water from 7 countries, with concentrations ranging from 0.2 to 300 ng/L. No studies on the occurrence of haloperidol in drinking water were found. Our data highlight that the occurrence of psychotropic drugs in drinking water is a growing global reality and also show a significant lack of research dedicated to the topic. Furthermore, the results of this scoping review reinforce the need to expand water quality monitoring, improve analytical techniques, invest in advanced water treatment technologies, and implement public policies on the proper disposal of medication and the control of drug pollution.

title: Processi ecofisiologici ed ecosistemici nei boschi vetusti
summary: I boschi vetusti rappresentano oggi un riferimento essenziale per orientare strategie adattative di gestione, conservazione e ripristino degli ecosistemi forestali: conservano grandi quantità di carbonio, ospitano biodiversità e mostrano pr
content: I boschi vetusti rappresentano oggi un riferimento essenziale per orientare strategie adattative di gestione, conservazione e ripristino degli ecosistemi forestali: conservano grandi quantità di carbonio, ospitano biodiversità e mostrano processi ecologici che nei boschi giovani o gestiti sono assenti o meno evidenti. Capire come funzionano aiuta a prevedere la stabilità futura delle foreste e la loro capacità di rispondere a siccità, aumento delle temperature e altri stress. Con l’aumento dell’età e delle dimensioni, gli alberi affrontano vincoli diversi da quelli delle piante giovani. Devono trasportare acqua più in alto, mantenere una maggiore massa viva e sostenere chiome complesse. Questi fattori possono ridurre la crescita e la produttività, sia del singolo albero sia dell’intero popolamento. A livello individuale, il rallentamento può dipendere da maggiori costi respiratori, limiti idraulici e minore efficienza fotosintetica. A livello di popolamento, può essere associato a minore disponibilità di nutrienti e a una maggiore allocazione di risorse verso componenti non legnose. Resta però incerto quanto questi processi causino davvero il declino produttivo osservato. Età, dimensioni, genetica, ambiente e disturbi interagiscono in modi ancora poco chiari, limitando la capacità di prevedere la risposta delle foreste vetuste al cambiamento globale.

title: Prototyping Chain-Elongation-Mediated Dehalogenation for Groundwater Bioremediation
summary: Abstract Chlorinated ethenes are widespread groundwater contaminants. Microbial reductive dehalogenation can detoxify chlorinated ethenes but requires sustained H2 delivery to organohalide-respiring bacteria. In enrichment cultures, microbi
content: Abstract Chlorinated ethenes are widespread groundwater contaminants. Microbial reductive dehalogenation can detoxify chlorinated ethenes but requires sustained H2 delivery to organohalide-respiring bacteria. In enrichment cultures, microbial chain elongation was shown to reliably provide H2 for dehalogenation from the conversion of ethanol and acetate to butyrate and caproate and subsequent fermentation of these carboxylates. Supported by robust laboratory testing, here, we document the first field-scale application of chain elongation-mediated dehalogenation in chlorinated ethene-contaminated groundwater. Native groundwater communities produced mainly propionate from ethanol and acetate in microcosms and the field, whereas bioaugmentation with a chain-elongating enrichment culture redirected microbial metabolism toward butyrate production and supported dehalogenation to ethene. Dehalogenation was favored at a lower organic carbon loading (900 mg C L–1 either as ethanol + acetate, butyrate, or caproate). Chain elongation was more strongly stimulated at higher ethanol to acetate molar ratios and organic carbon loadings (3500 mg C L–1). Bioaugmentation with chain-elongating bacteria in groundwater produced detectable butyrate concentrations, increased the molar ratio of ethene and ethane from 0.20 to 0.51 during monitoring, and did not stimulate methanogenesis. This study positions chain elongation-mediated dehalogenation as an effective strategy for groundwater bioremediation of chlorinated ethenes.

title: Enhancing waste management sustainability in Kuwait’s oil sector through artificial intelligence: A comparative analysis and framework development
summary: environment (KOC, 2025).Despite its economic importance, Kuwait's oil industry faces growing environmental challenges (Al-Barood et al., 2024;Alameedy et al., 2026).The sector produces large amounts of hazardous solid, liquid, and gaseous w
content: environment (KOC, 2025).Despite its economic importance, Kuwait's oil industry faces growing environmental challenges (Al-Barood et al., 2024;Alameedy et al., 2026).The sector produces large amounts of hazardous solid, liquid, and gaseous waste.This happens across exploration, drilling, extraction, refining, and transport (Manikumar et al., 2024).Waste streams include produced water, brine discharge, drilling residues, oil sludge, contaminated soil, gas flaring emissions, sour gases, and greenhouse gases.These threaten soil, groundwater, marine life, and air quality (AlRukaibi and AlSalem, 2022).Produced water is the largest waste stream from oil operations in Enhancing waste management sustainability in Kuwait's oil sector through artificial intelligence: A comparative analysis and framework development

title: Parasitism induces negative effects of clonal integration in the invasive plant Sphagneticola trilobata regardless of nutrient heterogeneity
summary: Introduction Clonal integration typically enhances the fitness of clonal plants in heterogeneous resource environments, whereas it reduces fitness under parasitic stress. However, it remains unclear whether parasitic stress interacts with n
content: Introduction Clonal integration typically enhances the fitness of clonal plants in heterogeneous resource environments, whereas it reduces fitness under parasitic stress. However, it remains unclear whether parasitic stress interacts with nutrient heterogeneity to affect the ecological effects of clonal integration. Methods We conducted a greenhouse pot experiment using the invasive clonal plant Sphagneticola trilobata , with or without one ramet parasitized by Cuscuta chinensis , and with or without severing the connection (allowing or preventing integration), under heterogeneous or homogeneous nutrient supply, combined with 15 N tracing. Results and discussion Our results showed that (1) compared with the severed treatment, the connection treatment significantly increased C. chinensis biomass and markedly decreased the biomass of connected but unparasitized ramets, but did not affect the biomass of directly parasitized ramets, ultimately leading to a significant decrease in the total biomass of clonal fragments of S. trilobata ; (2) heterogeneous nutrient supply significantly intensified the detrimental effect of C. chinensis on parasitized ramets, but did not significantly affect connected unparasitized ramets; and (3) neither nutrient heterogeneity nor parasitism by C. chinensis affected the amount of 15 N translocated among ramets. Collectively, these findings indicate that under parasitic stress, clonal integration has detrimental effects on plant fitness. Nutrient heterogeneity intensified the negative effects on parasitized ramets in poor patches but did not alter the detrimental effects on whole clonal fragments. Thus, C. chinensis suppresses S. trilobata consistently across nutrient conditions, supporting its potential as a biocontrol agent.

title: Solving calibration and reanalysis challenges of ocean biogeochemical dynamics with neural schemes: a 1D vertical model case-study
summary: Abstract. Numerous studies in climate and ocean sciences have highlighted the crucial role of ocean biogeochemical (BGC) models in studying and monitoring the global carbon cycle. Despite major advances due to both modelling and observation
content: Abstract. Numerous studies in climate and ocean sciences have highlighted the crucial role of ocean biogeochemical (BGC) models in studying and monitoring the global carbon cycle. Despite major advances due to both modelling and observation efforts, the quantification and reduction of the uncertainties in ocean BGC processes remain a key challenge. These difficulties arise primarily from the scarcity of observational datasets and the considerable uncertainties in ocean physics. Current ocean physics reanalyses still struggle to accurately represent the ocean’s complex dynamics, particularly at small scales, which play a critical role in driving biogeochemical cycles. Consequently, the performance of operational ocean data assimilation (DA) systems remains limited when applied to BGC dynamics, both for model calibration and reanalysis applications. Here, we explore machine learning approaches to address these challenges. To this end, we develop an Observing System Simulation Experiment (OSSE) framework for 1D ocean BGC dynamics, designed for both training and benchmarking purposes. We rely on a differentiable programming code of a 1D Nitrate-Ammonium-Phytoplankton-Zooplankton-Detritus (NNPZD) ocean BGC model forced by solar irradiance and vertical mixing. The proposed OSSE incorporates location-dependent uncertainties in physical forcings and considers realistic configurations of in situ observing systems. Based on these OSSEs, we design numerical experiments addressing both the calibration of model parameters, the reconstruction of 1D ocean BGC dynamics and the reduction of the uncertainties in the physical forcings. For calibration and inversion, we investigate a model-based variational DA scheme, an end-to-end deep learning scheme and their hybrid combination. Our results demonstrate the potential of learning-based schemes to substantially reduce calibration uncertainties and improve physical forcing estimates. When coupled with a variational DA scheme, this approach yields enhanced reconstructions of ocean BGC dynamics. Sensitivity analyses with respect to forcing uncertainties and observing system configurations provide insights into how these findings could be extended to real-world ocean BGC modelling and monitoring.

title: Modeling Resilience of the Earth System Under Climate Change Mitigation
summary: Human livelihoods rely on the ability of the Earth system to buffer greenhouse gas emissions and recover from externally forced and internal disturbances to a dynamic equilibrium. Anthropogenic climate change and human action challenge this
content: Human livelihoods rely on the ability of the Earth system to buffer greenhouse gas emissions and recover from externally forced and internal disturbances to a dynamic equilibrium. Anthropogenic climate change and human action challenge this resilience of climate, carbon cycle, and ecosystems to disturbances. Therefore, assessing how they affect the future trajectory of the Earth system is critical for adaptation and mitigation planning. Comprehensive Earth system projections are foundational for these assessments. However, they mostly neglect the explicit effects of anthropogenic interventions for stabilizing global climate like artificial carbon dioxide (CO2) removal and deliberate stratospheric aerosol injections. The projections also rarely account for impacts of varying volcanic aerosol levels on climate and carbon cycle. Their accuracy in simulating repercussions of climate extremes on vegetation productivity, an essential carbon sink, also remains unclear. These shortcomings compromise the reliability of long-term risk assessments. This dissertation, based on three manuscripts, explores ways to better represent vegetation resilience, disturbances from volcanic eruptions, and human interventions in projections of climate change mitigation scenarios. To this end, the work includes model development, statistical emulation, and comparisons of models and observations. As part of this work, Earth system model simulations with an explicitly represented, renewable-powered approach for CO2 removal and conversion corroborate the absence of unintended side effects that would substantially offset its removal potential. However, the results also reveal fundamental land use constraints that could cause target conflicts between large-scale CO2 removal, agriculture, and ecosystem services. Further, model emulations with varying volcanic aerosol levels demonstrate that representing this intermittent forcing realistically increases global and regional temperature uncertainty relative to a constant approach commonly applied in climate change assessments. The results suggest a substantial share of this uncertainty propagates to natural carbon sinks. This significantly increases uncertainty about when planetary temperatures may stabilize, and net-zero emissions may be reached, making it vital to better account for varying aerosol levels in future risk assessments. Finally, comparing statistical relationships between temperature--moisture and vegetation productivity extremes in observations and two Earth system models provides confidence in modeled vegetation resilience at regional to global scales. Both models perform worse locally and struggle to match the observed timing between hydroclimatic drivers and vegetation responses. Recalibrating and improving process models could reduce these discrepancies which may be caused by high biases in soil moisture rates of change. Findings from the studies are limited by uncertain and ambiguous scenarios of socioeconomic

title: Saving space for the long now: old-growth forests and ancient trees in the Anthropocene
summary: Old-growth forests and ancient trees embody a profound temporal and spatial otherness that stands in stark contrast to the accelerated, unmoored rhythms of Anthropocene human societies. This paper bridges dendrological science, environmenta
content: Old-growth forests and ancient trees embody a profound temporal and spatial otherness that stands in stark contrast to the accelerated, unmoored rhythms of Anthropocene human societies. This paper bridges dendrological science, environmental philosophy, and conservation policy to argue that arboreal life constitutes an irreplaceable form of non-human being requiring deliberate, multi-scale protection. It first distinguishes between old-growth forest ecosystems that form complex collective networks perceived culturally as both sacred sanctuary and forbidding wilderness and solitary ancient heritage trees, widely venerated as individual touchstones of deep time embedded often within human landscapes. Drawing on recent physiological research, the paper introduces the framework of dendromorphism: the modular, adaptive, indeterminate growth pattern of trees that escapes programmed senescence, accumulates heritable somatic mutations, and sustains a youthful living envelope over ancient structural biomass. This unique biology produces organisms that integrate centuries of environmental experience within a single permanently rooted existence. Situating the argument within a 4,000-year cultural arc from the Epic of Gilgamesh to the Long Now Foundation, the paper concludes with three actionable conservation strategies: strict old-growth forest preservation, systematic stewardship of ancient heritage trees, and intentional landscape-wide recruitment of successor tree cohorts to sustain arboreal deep time into future millennia.

title: Timing matters: earlier planting leads to increased seedling emergence success in Zostera marina seeds
summary: Globally seagrass restoration efforts have been increasing in recent years. Seed-based restoration is often favoured, as it provides higher genetic diversity and less impact on donor meadows. Restoration success is highly dependent on site-
content: Globally seagrass restoration efforts have been increasing in recent years. Seed-based restoration is often favoured, as it provides higher genetic diversity and less impact on donor meadows. Restoration success is highly dependent on site-selection, methods and timing. To increase the success of seedling establishment for restoration programmes we carried out experiments investigating timing, planting methods and sediment type under semi-controlled conditions in a mesocosm setup. In December, February and March Zostera marina seeds were placed in hessian bags or directly into the sediment in small boxes. Both set ups contained two different types of sediment, one coming from our donor meadow (SG) and one from an unvegetated beach (noSG). Our experiments showed that the Zostera marina population from Porthdinllaen, North Wales, is a winter seedling emergence population. Seedling establishment was most successful at the lowest temperature in December when planted directly into the sediment (43.2 ± 8.1%). Planting time and method had a significant effect on seedling emergence. The use of hessian bags decreased seedling emergence to 23 ± 6% in December and down to 0.8 ± 1.4% in March. Hessian bags in March were covered in epiphytic algae. Sediment type furthermore had a significant effect on the leaf length; 6.4 ± 1.2 (SG) to 3.7 ± 0.86 (noSG) cm in December and 3.79 ± 0.64 (SG) to 3.02 ± 0.82 (noSG) cm in March. The presented results here could have important implications for success of restorations activities.

title: An n-FET-only IGZO low-dropout regulator evaluated under practical power-management conditions
summary: Power-management circuits remain underdeveloped in flexible electronics, limiting autonomous sensing and control systems. Thin-film transistor low-dropout (LDO) regulators have demonstrated voltage regulation beyond silicon, but standalone
content: Power-management circuits remain underdeveloped in flexible electronics, limiting autonomous sensing and control systems. Thin-film transistor low-dropout (LDO) regulators have demonstrated voltage regulation beyond silicon, but standalone metrics alone do not show whether foundry-enabled IGZO regulators can support practical low-power rails. We report an n-FET-only IGZO low-dropout regulator evaluated as a power-management block, not only as a standalone circuit. The regulator operates from a 3.3 V rail with quiescent current close to 1 µA and provides reference-set local regulation for low-power sensing electronics. The measurements show three relevant limits for practical use: chip-to-chip output-voltage variability, with standard deviation of approximately 98–125 mV across the load range, simulation-to-measurement discrepancies under headroom-limited operation, and output-voltage drift during 24 h fixed-bias operation. Finally, the fabricated regulator replaced a commercial LDO in one solar-powered sensing node, achieving a similar operating time, while the output drift limits its use as a general-purpose replacement.

title: Measuring atmospheric microplastic composition and occurrence from an uncrewed aerial system
summary: Airborne microplastic (MP) particles are transported through the atmosphere, yet direct measurements at altitude remain scarce. We developed a novel uncrewed aerial system (UAS)-based method for in situ MP sampling within and above the atmo
content: Airborne microplastic (MP) particles are transported through the atmosphere, yet direct measurements at altitude remain scarce. We developed a novel uncrewed aerial system (UAS)-based method for in situ MP sampling within and above the atmospheric boundary layer. In this proof-of-concept study, we deployed the UAS at 80–100 m above ground level (a.g.l.) in Colorado, USA, during fall 2024, collecting particles larger than 1 µm at two sites with high anthropogenic activity using an environmental cyclone sampler. Airborne particles were isolated, counted by optical microscopy, and identified by Raman microscopy with automated spectral analysis (OpenSpecy). Spectroscopically confirmed MPs were detected at 100 m a.g.l. and represented a mean of 13.8 ± 1.8% of the blank-corrected, morphologically selected airborne-particle counts for particles in the 3–10 µm size range. Hetero-aggregates dominated the samples, consistent with traffic-related material. This proof of concept demonstrates the feasibility of UAS-based atmospheric MP sampling and establishes a framework adaptable for ocean-surface, high-altitude, and remote environment monitoring.

title: Quantifying coastal ocean anthropogenic carbon changes and their uncertainties
summary: Abstract Despite recent progress in quantifying anthropogenic carbon (C anth ) in global oceans, coastal regions remain understudied due to methodological and observational challenges. Here, we develop and generalize a Regional rEgression–b
content: Abstract Despite recent progress in quantifying anthropogenic carbon (C anth ) in global oceans, coastal regions remain understudied due to methodological and observational challenges. Here, we develop and generalize a Regional rEgression–based Coastal Anthropogenic carbon estimation algorithm (RECA) designed specifically for coastal environments. Regional rEgression–based Coastal Anthropogenic carbon estimation algorithm builds upon the extended multiple linear regression framework, incorporating adaptations such as improved regression construction strategies, optimized data selection, and reduced subjectivity in decision‐making, creating a unified approach across diverse coastal settings. Using synthetic datasets with known ∆C anth from global ocean biogeochemical model simulations across multiple North American coastal regions, we estimate that the uncertainty of RECA is about 3.25 μ mol kg −1 . We also compare RECA with two other regression‐based algorithms, originally developed for the open ocean, to evaluate their performance in coastal environments after some adaptations. All three approaches have similar biases but different strengths, underscoring the importance of using a consistent method. An ensemble approach combining these three algorithms modestly improves reconstruction fidelity, but at the cost of increased complexity. We also evaluate the contributions of non‐steady‐state variations of both natural and C anth components because uncertainty about these components has long challenged the interpretation of regression‐based ∆C anth results. We find that the algorithms indeed remove most, but not all, of the natural variations and appear to capture some, but not all, of the non‐steady‐state C anth . This methodological framework provides a robust, broadly applicable, and easy‐to‐implement tool for estimating coastal ∆C anth with uncertainty quantification, allowing us to more confidently track C anth accumulation in a changing dynamic coastal ocean.

title: Modelling wellbore scaling in geothermal systems using a coupled hydrodynamic–geochemical simulator
summary: Flow in geothermal wells is characterised by strong variations in pressure ( P ), temperature ( T ), and flow velocity ( V ). These changes can drive the fluid into supersaturation with respect to specific mineral phases, leading to scale d
content: Flow in geothermal wells is characterised by strong variations in pressure ( P ), temperature ( T ), and flow velocity ( V ). These changes can drive the fluid into supersaturation with respect to specific mineral phases, leading to scale deposition on pipe walls. Scale growth modifies the pressure–temperature distribution inside the well and progressively alters scale thickness and mineralogy. Increased hydraulic resistance reduces the flow rate, thereby lowering the efficiency of heat extraction ( Gunnarsson and Arnórsson, 2005 , Zarrouk et al., 2014 ). We develop a multi-feed-zone, transient wellbore scaling simulator that uniquely integrates, within a single openly available framework, (1) transient two-phase wellbore flow, (2) multi-mineral equilibrium and kinetic geochemistry through a coupling to PHREEQC, and (3) the feedback of scale growth on conduit geometry and wall roughness. This enables the coupled spatio-temporal evolution of scale thickness, mineralogy, and wellhead conditions to be simulated for a specified feed-zone chemistry, mineral assemblage, set of deposition rates, and production protocol. Applied to Krafla well KJ-9, the model reproduces the calcite scale location inferred from caliper logs. Simulations of the simultaneous deposition of calcite, anhydrite and quartz yield scale compositions that are zoned in both the vertical and radial directions.

title: A multi-step sequential pretreatment for boosting biomass conversion
summary: This study aims to overcome the structural recalcitrance of lignocellulosic biomass and improve the economic viability of biorefineries. A multi-step sequential pretreatment strategy combining hydrothermal pretreatment, twin-screw extrusion
content: This study aims to overcome the structural recalcitrance of lignocellulosic biomass and improve the economic viability of biorefineries. A multi-step sequential pretreatment strategy combining hydrothermal pretreatment, twin-screw extrusion, and deep eutectic solvent (DES) treatments was developed to effectively deconstruct poplar biomass while recovering high-quality lignin, xylooligosaccharides (XOS), and fermentable sugars.The results demonstrated that this integrated approach achieved exceptional pretreatment performance, with 89.7% delignification and 85.3% xylan removal. The strategy enabled near-complete cellulose enzymatic hydrolysis at a low enzyme loading (15 FPU/g) and achieved a 45.7% XOS yield. Furthermore, the process yielded high-purity lignin (99.9%) with an 81.5% recovery rate,characterized by reduced molecular weight, enhanced antioxidant activity (IC 50 = 56.16 mg/L), and a high phenolic hydroxyl content (2.81 mmol/g).This sequential pretreatment strategy exhibits significant potential for the integrated valorization of poplar biomass into fermentable monosaccharides, functional oligosaccharides, and antioxidant lignin derivatives, advancing the sustainability of lignocellulosic biorefineries.

title: Peat Soil Chemistry–Maize Productivity Correlations under Red Mud and Goat Manure Amendments
summary: Peat soils are characterized by high acidity, low base saturation, and complex nutrient dynamics, making relationships between soil chemical properties and maize productivity important to evaluate under different amendment regimes. This stu
content: Peat soils are characterized by high acidity, low base saturation, and complex nutrient dynamics, making relationships between soil chemical properties and maize productivity important to evaluate under different amendment regimes. This study aimed to explore these relationships under combinations of red mud and goat manure. The experiment was conducted for three months using peat soil from North Pontianak District, Pontianak City, Indonesia, in a 4 × 3 factorial arrangement with four red mud rates (100, 200, 300, and 400 g/polybag) and three goat manure rates (1,000, 2,000, and 3,000 g/polybag), with three replications (36 experimental units). Pearson correlation analysis explored relationships between soil pH, organic C, total N, available P, exchangeable K, Ca, Mg, and Na, cation exchange capacity, base saturation, and maize grain weight and number per cob. Correlation patterns varied among amendment combinations. Nominal associations were observed for pH, exchangeable Ca, K, and Na with grain number or weight in several combinations, while available P and cation exchange capacity were associated with grain weight in selected treatments. Overall, the observed relationships were combination-specific. Because each combination had only three replications and multiple correlations were examined, these findings should be interpreted as exploratory. Further studies with greater replication and factorial analysis are needed to confirm the observed relationships.

title: PLANT WATER-CARBON RELATIONS IN HUANGLONGBING-AFFECTED CITRUS TREES AND THE IMPACT OF HLB EXPOSURE DURATION, FRUIT DEVELOPMENTAL STAGE, AND SOURCE-SINK MANIPULATION ON THESE RELATIONS
summary: Bulk phloem flow is driven by pressure gradients generated by water drawn from the xylem, coupling source-sink transport with water status. Huanglongbing (HLB), a phloem-affecting bacterial disease of citrus, disrupts phloem transport, and
content: Bulk phloem flow is driven by pressure gradients generated by water drawn from the xylem, coupling source-sink transport with water status. Huanglongbing (HLB), a phloem-affecting bacterial disease of citrus, disrupts phloem transport, and causes canopy water deficit. Although improved water management can enhance HLB-affected tree health, the effects of HLB on water-driven source-sink relations are unknown. Fruits function as both carbon sink and water reservoir, but the role of fruit in regulating whole-tree water status remain poorly understood. We examined leaf-fruit water relations in HLB-affected citrus and evaluated how HLB exposure duration, fruit developmental stage, and source-sink manipulation shape these dynamics. Source-sink relations were manipulated in branches of symptomatic trees with long-term (four years) and recent (six months) HLB exposure. We girdled branches with a single fruit as the sink and defoliated at (0%, 50%, or 75%), and an ungirdled, non-defoliated branch served as control. We measured stomatal conductance, leaf hydraulic traits, leaf and fruit soluble sugars, diurnal fruit shrinkage (to estimate xylem backflow) and fruit water loss. Source-sink manipulation did not affect shoot total soluble sugar. HLB-exposure resulted in less negative osmotic potential, more negative turgor potential and reduced modulus of elasticity and relative water content at turgor loss point. HLB exposure also increased diurnal fruit shrinkage, with shrinkage responses to source-sink manipulation varying across fruit development stages. Collectively, these findings suggest that long-term HLB exposure promotes leaf acclimation to water deficits, however, high sink demand may diminish the leaf water status regulation at Stage II, when fruit sink carbon demand is highest.

title: Removal of fecal bacteria by fast-flowing foam filters for biological swimming pool filtration
summary: ABSTRACT Biological swimming pools rely on efficient removal of fecal bacteria and pathogens. Here we report on results from a bacterial addition experiment, in which Escherichia coli (E. coli), Enterococcus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (P. a
content: ABSTRACT Biological swimming pools rely on efficient removal of fecal bacteria and pathogens. Here we report on results from a bacterial addition experiment, in which Escherichia coli (E. coli), Enterococcus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (P. aeruginosa) were introduced into two swimming pools, one with and one without a biological filter. The biological filter was based on polyurethane (PU) mats with a high surface to volume ratio. Biofilters provided a solid removal of fecal bacteria (E. coli and Enterococcus) with removal rates exceeding 50% (Log10 0.3) per filter passage, while the removal rate of P. aeruginosa was lower (43%). The area-specific removal of E. coli was more than 5 times higher for the PU foam filter than for typical Slow Sand Filters. Finally, we evaluated the hypothesis that a biofilter colonized by biofilm may act as a reservoir for fecal pathogens. We observed limited survival of pathogens in the biofilter 41 and 156 days after the additions, while most added cells were removed, suggesting minimal risk to swimmers under the tested conditions. PU foam-based biofilters appear to be a promising technology for pathogen reduction in biological swimming pools, while mitigating negative impacts of chlorine use, such as toxicity and potential carcinogenic effects.

title: Multiscale pH fluctuations on a stable algal reef community (SE Sardinia, Tyrrhenian Sea)
summary: The Mediterranean Sea is threatened by ocean acidification and warming, in combination with habitat loss, pollution, invasive species, and overexploitation. Assessing local high-frequency pH variability in the context of relevant basin-scal
content: The Mediterranean Sea is threatened by ocean acidification and warming, in combination with habitat loss, pollution, invasive species, and overexploitation. Assessing local high-frequency pH variability in the context of relevant basin-scale time series data is essential to understand ecosystem vulnerability. We report the results of the Italian national pH monitoring based on the Marine Strategy Framework Directive, and the pH dynamics observed at Capo Carbonara. An experimental station equipped with a pH sensor and CTD probe was deployed at 32 m depth on a sandy bottom bordered by Coralligenous assemblages. Physical and biogeochemical variables were continuously recorded over 345 days and analyzed through additive time series decomposition. The benthic assemblages were surveyed by photographic and destructive sampling in summer and autumn 2016 and spring 2017 on algal reef and sandy bottom, to describe the biological components undergoing and contributing to the pH fluctuations. Seasonal pH variability ranged up to 0.2 units annually and 0.1 units daily, with maxima in January and minima in August, while the range of pH on the basin scale had higher mean values and exceeded local variability. Assemblage changes were driven by algal turf development and the invasive Caulerpa cylindracea . Coralligenous taxa appear stable, despite the substantial natural pH variability, shaped by meteo-marine conditions, water mass circulation, Saharan dust inputs, and benthic biological processes, with primary producers and calcifiers exerting a key influence. The ongoing trend of increasing temperatures and decreasing pH may threaten the Coralligenous ability to cope with the shifting future boundaries of such variability.

title: Strong growing season soil methane uptake observed in a restored prairie-savanna
summary: Humid tallgrass prairies in the Upper Midwest have been largely converted to agriculture, creating large regional sources of greenhouse gases through soil oxidation and nutrient enrichment. Although prairie restoration is expanding, greenho
content: Humid tallgrass prairies in the Upper Midwest have been largely converted to agriculture, creating large regional sources of greenhouse gases through soil oxidation and nutrient enrichment. Although prairie restoration is expanding, greenhouse gas fluxes from restored ecosystems remain poorly quantified. We measured growing season soil carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide fluxes across restored oak woodland, open tallgrass prairie, and wet prairie at Nachusa Grasslands, Illinois, and tested how fluxes were controlled by soil temperature, moisture, cover type, and elevation, and associations with surface soil microbial communities. Across all cover types, soils were consistent carbon dioxide sources (median 2.29 μmol m-2 s-1), methane sinks (median −0.36 nmol m-2 s-1), and neutral for nitrous oxide. Woodland soils were exceptionally strong methane sinks, while open prairie was often near neutral. Notably, net methane emission was absent even in wet prairie. Decision tree models explained 50%–70% of variability in carbon dioxide and methane fluxes, with soil temperature as the dominant control on carbon dioxide and cover type plus soil moisture most important for methane uptake. Inferred microbial community composition was dominated by putative aerobic taxa, including decomposers, nitrogen cyclers, and methane oxidizers. These results indicate that restored Midwest prairie-savanna ecosystems likely function as net greenhouse gas sinks, with particularly high rates of methane uptake in woodlands. Future work should incorporate non-growing season fluxes and vegetation fluxes to develop full ecosystem greenhouse gas budgets and better quantify the climate mitigation potential of prairie restoration.

title: A unifying principle linking water uptake and nutrient delivery in trees with implications for soilless vascular delivery
summary: Tree productivity, orchard sustainability and dryland reforestation are constrained simultaneously by water scarcity and nutrient losses. Here a unifying nutrient-water principle is developed for woody plants. The principle states that the
content: Tree productivity, orchard sustainability and dryland reforestation are constrained simultaneously by water scarcity and nutrient losses. Here a unifying nutrient-water principle is developed for woody plants. The principle states that the minimum soil-derived flow compatible with a specified plant state is the greater of a hydraulic baseline and the flow needed to deliver the limiting nutrient. For nutrient i , internal delivery is represented locally as J i = η i C i Q s + I i , where C i is effective root-zone concentration, Q s is soil-derived flow, η i is an effective soil-to-xylem transfer coefficient and I i is direct vascular input. The formulation predicts a hyperbolic decline in nutrient-driven flow requirement with increasing balanced nutrient concentration, control by the most limiting nutrient and strong leverage from efficient delivery when soil losses are high. Controlled split-root and hydroponic studies demonstrate rapid nutrient-hydraulic coupling, while ecosystem, tree and orchard observations are consistent with the predicted importance of nutrient balance. Published injection studies support targeted vascular correction of selected nutrient deficiencies and provide a basis for evaluating broader soilless delivery. The principle links plant hydraulics and mineral nutrition in a concise, quantitative and testable framework and identifies experiments needed to determine its parameters and practical limits.

title: Vermicompost-assisted Azotobacter and Bacillus inoculation enables partial substitution of mineral NPK and improves maize yield, nutrient uptake, soil fertility, and biological activity
summary: Reducing dependence on mineral fertilizers requires integrated nutrient management (INM) strategies that sustain maize productivity while improving soil functioning. A field experiment evaluated nine combinations of mineral NPK, farmyard ma
content: Reducing dependence on mineral fertilizers requires integrated nutrient management (INM) strategies that sustain maize productivity while improving soil functioning. A field experiment evaluated nine combinations of mineral NPK, farmyard manure, vermicompost, and Azotobacter - Bacillus inoculation in a randomized block design with three replications. The 75% NPK treatments integrated with either FYM or vermicompost and inoculation formed the leading treatment group. T7 (75% NPK + 5 t vermicompost ha⁻¹ + Azotobacter – Bacillus ) recorded the highest observed grain yield (40.8 q ha⁻¹), stover yield (62.5 q ha⁻¹), and total N, P, and K uptake (121.0, 31.3, and 92.2 kg ha⁻¹, respectively), but these responses did not differ significantly from T6. Microbial biomass carbon and dehydrogenase activity were also highest under T7 (112 mg kg⁻¹ and 4.4 µg TPF g⁻¹ h⁻¹, respectively) and remained statistically comparable with T6. Available soil K was the only variable across nutrient uptake, soil fertility, micronutrient availability, and biological activity that differed significantly between T7 and T6. Relative to sole 100% NPK, T7 increased microbial biomass carbon by 32.9% and dehydrogenase activity by 51.7%. T7 generated gross returns of ₹99,340 ha⁻¹ (US$1,263.79 ha⁻¹), net returns of ₹59,722 ha⁻¹ (US$759.78 ha⁻¹), and economic efficiency of ₹567.66 ha⁻¹ day⁻¹ (US$7.22 ha⁻¹ day⁻¹). Principal component analysis associated the 75% NPK-based treatments with greater water-holding capacity, soil organic carbon, nutrient availability, and microbial activity. Thus, the complete 75% NPK-based organic-biological treatment packages provided effective fertilizer-saving options under the tested conditions.

title: Climate Litigation and Democracy in Bangladesh
summary: Climate litigation is emerging as an important avenue for addressing environmental harms and strengthening accountability in India. As climate-related challenges intensify, courts are increasingly being called upon to consider how constitut
content: Climate litigation is emerging as an important avenue for addressing environmental harms and strengthening accountability in India. As climate-related challenges intensify, courts are increasingly being called upon to consider how constitutional rights, environmental protection, and democratic governance intersect. This case study examines the evolving climate litigation landscape in India and explores its implications for public participation, access to justice, and government accountability. It is part of a series on climate litigation and democracy in Asia and the Pacific, which examines how legal action is shaping participation, accountability, and rights-based responses to climate change.

title: Consistent estimates of carbonyl sulfide and methane stratospheric lifetimes retrieved from AirCore profiles at different latitudes
summary: Abstract. Stratospheric loss is a major sink for both carbonyl sulfide (COS) and methane (CH4), but their stratospheric lifetimes and sinks remain poorly constrained because high-resolution observations of their vertical distributions in th
content: Abstract. Stratospheric loss is a major sink for both carbonyl sulfide (COS) and methane (CH4), but their stratospheric lifetimes and sinks remain poorly constrained because high-resolution observations of their vertical distributions in the lower stratosphere are sparse. Here, we estimate the mean stratospheric lifetime and sink of COS and CH4 from their correlations with N2O using two distinct methods applied to AirCore vertical profile measurements from three Northern Hemisphere summer campaigns. From these profiles, we derive a COS stratospheric lifetime of 69–90 years, corresponding to a sink of 30–41 GgS yr-1. For CH4, we find a stratospheric lifetime of 149–168 years, corresponding to a sink of 23–26 TgC yr-1. These values are in good agreement with previous estimates (39–76 years for COS, 152–160 years for CH4) and with estimates based on ACE-FTS observations (75–76 years for COS, 146–172 years for CH4). As has been noted previously, we also find a decline in the COS tropospheric burden between 2016 and 2020 in our AirCore samples, in contrast to the continued growth of CH4 and N2O. In addition, we found that tracer-tracer correlations vary among flights, and even within the same campaign, pointing to variability in lower-stratospheric composition. Although this variability may reflect differences in stratospheric transport, its origin remains unclear and requires further investigation. These results provide observational constraints on the stratospheric budgets of COS and CH4 and help refine their representation in atmospheric chemistry and transport models.

title: On-line analysis of N 2 O isotopic composition during biological nitrogen removal in wastewater treatment to disentangle production and reduction processes
summary: Abstract. Nitrous oxide (N2O) is a potent greenhouse gas, and emissions from wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) represent a significant and highly variable source. Understanding the dynamics in microbial pathways of N2O formation and reduc
content: Abstract. Nitrous oxide (N2O) is a potent greenhouse gas, and emissions from wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) represent a significant and highly variable source. Understanding the dynamics in microbial pathways of N2O formation and reduction during biological nitrogen removal is essential for targeted mitigation strategies. Stable isotope analysis of N2O (δ15Nα, δ15Nβ, δ18O, and 15N site preference) provides a powerful tool to disentangle and quantify N2O production and reduction processes, yet conventional analytical approaches lack temporal resolution. Here, we present the first long-term application of an off-axis integrated cavity output spectrometer for real-time N2O isotopic analysis at a pilot-scale WWTP over one year of operation. We developed a dynamic dilution system and implemented correction protocols for drift, N2O mole fraction dependence, and gas matrix effects on isotopic results, achieving uncertainties of 0.85 ‰ (δ15Nα), 1.08 ‰ (δ15Nβ), 0.81 ‰ (δ15Nbulk), 0.48 ‰ (δ18O) and 1.09 ‰ (15N site preference). Representative datasets demonstrate the system’s capability to (i) identify dominant N2O production pathways under standard operation, (ii) quantify N2O reduction in relation to dissolved oxygen concentration, and (iii) trace nitrogen transformation during low-level 15N-labelling experiments. Our results indicate nitrifier or heterotrophic denitrification as the main source of N2O, and that N2O reduction efficiency is strongly controlled by oxygen availability. This study highlights the potential of laser spectroscopy for continuous isotopic monitoring in real-world engineered systems and provides practical guidelines for uncertainty reduction and data interpretation. More specifically, our work forms a foundation for further investigations of the operational factors controlling N2O formation and N2O reduction in biological WWTPs and other complex anthropogenically-perturbed settings.

title: Deciphering efficient metabolic pathways in an anaerobic gut fungus coupled with a syntrophic methanogen
summary: Anaerobic gut fungi (AGF) are an integral part of the herbivore gut microbiome, primary decomposers of lignocellulose, and play a crucial role in establishing foundational links of syntrophic associations. The syntrophy with methanogens app
content: Anaerobic gut fungi (AGF) are an integral part of the herbivore gut microbiome, primary decomposers of lignocellulose, and play a crucial role in establishing foundational links of syntrophic associations. The syntrophy with methanogens appears beneficial for mitigating feedback inhibition and results in the augmentation of AGF activity. However, the thermodynamic advantages of the presence of methanogens to AGF remain poorly understood. This study explores the preferred pathways adopted by Cyllamyces sp. and Methanobrevibacter olleyae, using 13C-glucose as a substrate and spiked with malate and pyruvate in different experimental set-ups. The results indicated reduced biomass formation by Cyllamyces sp. in monoxenic culture with Methanobrevibacter olleyae compared to axenic AGF culture supplemented with glucose. Additionally, metabolic analyses revealed the pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase (PFO) as a key contributor to pyruvate metabolism. Malate supplementation notably enhanced the growth of Cyllamyces sp. and M. olleyae, whereas pyruvate supplementation enhanced the growth of Cyllamyces sp. only in axenic culture. This investigation provides insights into the preferred metabolic pathways operating in the hydrogenosomes of axenic anaerobic gut fungi (AGF) cultures and monoxenic AGF-methanogen co-cultures.

title: Economic Linkages and Multiplier Effects of Ethiopia’s Forest Sector and Wood Processing Industries: A Social Accounting Matrix -Based Analysis
summary: The economic contributions and intersectoral linkages of Ethiopia’s forest sector and its downstream wood processing industries have historically been undervalued in national policy frameworks. Utilizing the 2010 Social Accounting Matrix (S
content: The economic contributions and intersectoral linkages of Ethiopia’s forest sector and its downstream wood processing industries have historically been undervalued in national policy frameworks. Utilizing the 2010 Social Accounting Matrix (SAM) as a structural baseline framework, complemented by a mixed-methods approach including key informant interviews (KIIs), this study analyzes the structural dependencies and macroeconomic impacts of these interconnected sectors. The baseline analysis indicates that the forest sector accounted for 4.2% of Ethiopia’s GDP in 2010, highlighting a significant yet underutilized economic role. Linkage analyses suggest that the forest sector possesses strong forward and backward connections alongside a high reliance on domestic inputs, which aligns with its strategic potential to support inclusive development and circular economic transitions. Conversely, the downstream wood processing industry accounted for a minor share (0.04%) of GDP and exhibited a high dependency on imported inputs, which is associated with limitations in domestic value addition and circular resource loops. Multiplier simulations suggest that a one-dollar exogenous demand injection into the forest sector is associated with an income expansion of $1.94 within the sector itself and $0.93 in the downstream wood processing industry. Furthermore, the sectoral structure demonstrates a strong capacity for broad socio-economic distribution, particularly by supporting employment and income for unskilled labour, youth, women, and small urban households. These findings underscore the importance of prioritizing integrated forestry and wood-processing policies to leverage their structural potential for circular resource use and equitable growth.

title: Beyond exposure: Multifaceted pathways linking urban green space patterns to health in a hyper-dense urban core
summary: In hyper-dense urban cores, the traditional quantity–proximity paradigm is insufficient to explain urban green space (UGS)–health associations. Using Shanghai's Inner Ring as a case study, this study applies an observed-variable structural
content: In hyper-dense urban cores, the traditional quantity–proximity paradigm is insufficient to explain urban green space (UGS)–health associations. Using Shanghai's Inner Ring as a case study, this study applies an observed-variable structural path analysis guided by the Exposure–Perception–Behavior (EPB) framework to examine how UGS spatial patterns are associated with realized green contact, perception, behavioral processes, and self-rated physical and mental health. Neighborhood committee-scale UGS indicators were linked with individual health outcomes to estimate cross-sectional associations. UGS patterns were characterized across four dimensions—quantity, location, morphology, and distribution—and compared using dimension-specific and joint models. The results revealed heterogeneous spatial entry points but stable internal EPB associations. Quantity and distribution showed detectable positive total indirect associations with both physical and mental health; greater proximity to parks was directly associated with better mental health; and morphology showed associations with selected EPB components but no detectable total indirect association. The joint model showed that some UGS associations reflected shared information among correlated attributes, while connectivity-related associations remained stable across models. Restoration-related processes were associated with both health dimensions, whereas physical activity was more strongly associated with physical health and social interaction with mental health. These findings suggest that UGS–health associations in land-constrained urban cores cannot be fully understood through green provision or residential proximity alone. Instead, they require consideration of how spatial attributes relate to realized contact, perception, and behavioral processes. This study supports a pathway-sensitive diagnostic perspective for UGS planning.

title: Subsurface Carbon Discrepancies Drive Model Uncertainty in Wintertime Surface pCO2
summary: Anthropogenic carbon (Cant) uptake by the ocean is causing a dramatic rise in both the annual mean and seasonal cycle of surface ocean CO2 partial pressure (pCO2). These changes are significant because winter surface pCO2 trends heavily inf
content: Anthropogenic carbon (Cant) uptake by the ocean is causing a dramatic rise in both the annual mean and seasonal cycle of surface ocean CO2 partial pressure (pCO2). These changes are significant because winter surface pCO2 trends heavily influence the long-term ocean carbon sink trajectory. Cant-driven pCO2 increases are also amplified below the sea surface, where interior waters are weakly buffered due to large natural respiratory carbon burdens. Here, we use observation-based estimates and global ocean biogeochemical models to explore whether the wintertime entrainment of subsurface waters with amplified pCO2 into the surface mixed layer influences the evolution of winter surface pCO2. Specifically, we evaluate and compare ocean interior Cant-driven pCO2 change, focusing on the Pacific Ocean and the annual maximum mixed layer depth (MLDmax) globally. Observation-based analyses reveal that Cant-driven pCO2 changes at the MLDmax already outpace atmospheric pCO2 growth in some regions, confirming the translation of amplified subsurface signals into the winter mixed layer. However, models inconsistently capture these re-emergence patterns due to variable representations of subsurface buffering and vertical gradients in natural and anthropogenic dissolved inorganic carbon. The reemergence of amplified pCO2 provides evidence for a subsurface component to the ocean carbon cycle feedback modulated on seasonal timescales, with likely implications for the ocean carbon sink efficiency. Because pCO2 trends at the MLDmax are predicted to rapidly accelerate under moderate emissions, future projections require accurate representations of interior carbon distributions to better constrain winter surface pCO2 trends and their potential impact on the global ocean carbon sink strength.

title: Reframing Mangroves as Socio-Ecological Coastal Infrastructure: Development and Application of a Six-Pillar Socio-Ecological Infrastructure Framework
summary: Mangrove ecosystems are critical components of coastal socio-ecological systems, providing shoreline protection, biodiversity support, carbon sequestration, and livelihood opportunities for coastal communities. However, increasing pressures
content: Mangrove ecosystems are critical components of coastal socio-ecological systems, providing shoreline protection, biodiversity support, carbon sequestration, and livelihood opportunities for coastal communities. However, increasing pressures from climate change, coastal development, and environmental degradation threaten their resilience and long-term sustainability. This study proposes a Six-Pillar Socio-Ecological Infrastructure Framework that integrates ecological processes, climate regulation functions, coastal geomorphological dynamics, socio-economic interdependence, community co-management, and policy–climate governance. By synthesizing these interconnected dimensions, the framework provides a holistic analytical approach for understanding how mangrove ecosystems contribute to coastal resilience. Empirical insights from regions such as the Sundarbans and coastal areas of Gujarat illustrate the practical relevance of the framework for ecosystem-based adaptation and sustainable coastal governance. The manuscript also highlights policy implications, research gaps, and pathways for strengthening mangrove conservation within broader climate adaptation and coastal management strategies.

title: Reframing antimicrobial resistance as a land-system challenge through environmental pathways and climate interactions
summary: Abstract Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a planetary health challenge, yet land-system change remains overlooked. This review examines how agriculture, urbanisation, waste management, deforestation, aquaculture and climate-driven transiti
content: Abstract Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a planetary health challenge, yet land-system change remains overlooked. This review examines how agriculture, urbanisation, waste management, deforestation, aquaculture and climate-driven transitions shape resistance through altered input intensity, habitat reorganisation and enhanced connectivity. It identifies evidence gaps across vulnerable settings and proposes pathway-based surveillance, integrated datasets, longitudinal studies and coordinated interventions to reduce resistance selection, persistence and transmission across connected landscapes, informing research, policy and implementation.

title: SYSTEM FOR LAND-BASED EMISSIONS ESTIMATION IN KENYA(SLEEK) AND LAND-SECTOR CARBON ACCOUNTING IN KENYA: EVIDENCE FROM EMISSIONS AND REMOVALS ACCOUNTING, 1990-2015
source: International Journal of Science and Research Archive
